dialogs.title: Dialogue — Oskar på besök

notes: **Ju** — the most Swedish of all the small words. It means roughly "as we both know" or "you know": the speaker points to something the listener already knows or can see. *Mamma och pappa har **ju** en stuga* = "Mom and Dad have a cabin — you know that." It is never stressed and never starts a sentence. Say it quickly: **yü**.

**Väl** — "I assume so — right?" It turns a statement into a hopeful guess and invites agreement: *Du är **väl** helt slut?* (You must be exhausted, right?), *Du stannar **väl** till midsommar?* (You're staying, aren't you?). In Oskar's last line it shows mild resignation: *Jag följer **väl** med då* (I guess I'll come, then). **vehl**.
**Nog** — "probably, I think", a soft guess: *Det går **nog** bra*, *Det blir **nog** sol*. It's softer than *säkert* (surely) and more confident than *kanske* (maybe). **noog**.

**Ändå** — "anyway, still, after all": *Du kom **ju ändå**!* (You came after all!), *det är **ändå** jättemysigt* (it's still lovely). It marks a result that happens in spite of something. Stress on the second syllable: **en-DOH**. And **faktiskt** (**FAHK-tiskt**) — "actually" — adds a little surprise or correction, exactly like its English twin.

**Jo** — Elin answers Oskar's negative question (*blir det **inte**…?*) with *jo*, not *ja*. *Jo* means "yes" in reply to a question containing *inte*; *ja* would sound confused. English uses "yes" for both, often with an extra explanation ("Yes, there will"). **yoo**. And **nja** (**nyah**), a blend of *nej* and *ja*, means "well… not really" — perfect for hesitating politely.

**Liksom** — "like, sort of", the filler word of younger Swedes: *Jag har **liksom** inte bestämt mig*. Use it sparingly, as you would "like" in English. And **jätte-** (giant) in *jättemysigt* is a very common spoken prefix meaning "really, super": *jättebra*, *jättegott*, *jättetrött*.

grammars.title: Seven small words and what they add
body: None of these words changes the facts of a sentence. What they change is the **attitude**: how sure you are, whether you expect agreement, whether something is obvious or surprising. Leave them out and your Swedish is correct but a little stiff.
after: **Where they go:** in the sentence-adverb slot, the same place as *inte* — right after the finite verb in a normal main clause (*Det blir **nog** sol*), after the subject when it has been inverted (*Det kan du **ju** inte veta*). When two meet, the small word comes **first**, *inte* second: *Det kan du **ju inte** veta*, *Jag har **liksom inte** bestämt mig*.
In a subordinate clause they obey BIFF, just like *inte*, and stand **before** the verb: *…eftersom vi **ju** har en stuga*, *…att det **nog** blir sol*.
*Ju* and *väl* never stand first in a sentence. *Visst*, *faktiskt* and *ändå* can — and then the verb follows straight after: ***Visst** är det fint?*, ***Faktiskt** vet jag inte*.

grammars.title: Yes, no and everything in between
body: Swedes have a whole scale of answers between yes and no. These short replies are among the most frequent words in spoken Swedish.

after: *Jo* also appears at the start of a reply when you're about to explain or correct something: *Varför kom du inte? — **Jo**, alltså, bussen…* (Well, you see, the bus…).

blocks.text: A word of warning about **ju**: because it means "as you know", it can sound condescending if the other person doesn't actually know. *Det är ju enkelt!* (It's easy, obviously!) can come across as "Come on, everyone knows that." Use it with friends and for things that really are shared knowledge.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 12
items: *Nog* and *tro* go well together: *Jag tror att det **nog** blir bra.* (Note BIFF: *nog* before *blir*.)
Compare the three ways to express a guess: *Det blir **nog** sol* · *Jag **tror** att det blir sol* · *Det blir **kanske** sol*. Most sure to least sure: *nog* → *tror* → *kanske*.

sections.title: Polite Swedish without a word for "please"

blocks.text: Swedish has no everyday word for "please". *Snälla* exists, but it sounds pleading ("pretty please"), and *var så god* means "here you are". So how do Swedes make polite requests? With questions, with small words — and with *tack*.

head: How polite
Svenska
English
rows: Would you mind closing the door?

blocks.text: **Tack** does much of the work English gives to "please": *Ja, tack* (yes, please), *En kanelbulle, tack* (a cinnamon bun, please). Swedes also thank you for things that have already happened: *Tack för maten* (after a meal), *Tack för senast* (thanks for last time — said the next time you meet), *Tack för idag* (at the end of a class or a working day).
